items.definition: Equity financing of young high-potential companies, with high risk and an expectation of a large multiple.
items.example: A seed fund invests 2 M€ in a startup with no revenue yet.

items.definition: Management company that raises and manages the fund, makes investment decisions and earns fees and carry.
items.example: The GP decides to invest in a new portfolio company.

items.definition: Investor that commits capital to the fund without taking part in day-to-day management; liability is limited to its commitment.
items.example: A family office is an LP in three European VC funds.

items.definition: Individual investor who provides capital, time and network to startups, often at the earliest stages.
items.example: A former founder invests 100 k€ and opens their commercial network.

items.definition: Short programme providing capital, mentoring and resources to a cohort of startups, often in exchange for a small stake.
items.example: An accelerator takes 6% for a three-month programme.

items.definition: Capital raised but not yet invested by a fund, available for future deals or follow-ons.
items.example: The fund has 40 M€ of dry powder for the coming quarters.

items.definition: Set of investment opportunities received and qualified by a fund over a period.
items.example: The fund screens 300 deals a year and invests in six.

items.definition: Annual remuneration of the GP, usually a percentage of committed capital or fund value, covering management costs.
items.example: A 2% management fee on a 100 M€ fund is 2 M€ per year.

items.definition: Share of the fund's gains paid to the GP after LPs are repaid and the hurdle is cleared, often 20%.
items.example: The GP earns 20% of the profits above an 8% hurdle.

items.definition: Minimum return the fund must achieve before the GP receives carried interest.
items.example: With an 8% hurdle, the GP earns nothing until LPs reach that return.

items.definition: Rules for sharing the proceeds of a fund or an exit among LPs, the GP and shareholders, in a defined order.
items.example: The waterfall provides for capital repayment, then the hurdle, then carry.

items.definition: Return profile of a fund that starts negative because of fees and investments, then rises with exits.
items.example: The fund's IRR is negative in year 2 but positive in year 7.

items.definition: Year of a fund's first closing, used to compare performance across cohorts.
items.example: Vintage 2015 and 2021 funds are not comparable at the same stage.

items.definition: First external financing, often before product and revenue, to validate the team and the problem.
items.example: The startup raises 300 k€ in pre-seed to build a prototype.

items.definition: Financing round following pre-seed, funding early proof of traction and the commercial launch.
items.example: The 2 M€ seed funds the first sales hires.

items.definition: First significant institutional round, meant to fund repeatable growth after initial traction.
items.example: The 8 M€ Series A funds commercial expansion.

items.definition: Short financing between two rounds to extend runway until a next event.
items.example: A 1 M€ bridge adds six months of runway.

items.definition: Financing contract granting the right to shares at a future round, with no interest or maturity, often with a cap or discount.
items.example: A 500 k€ SAFE with a 5 M€ cap.

items.definition: Debt that converts into shares at a future round, with interest, maturity, cap and sometimes a discount.
items.example: The convertible note carries 5% interest and a 6 M€ cap.

items.definition: Company valuation before the round's capital is injected.
items.example: An 8 M€ pre-money with 2 M€ raised gives a 10 M€ post-money.

items.definition: Company valuation after the round's capital is injected; the base for computing the investor's share.
items.example: The investor's share is 2 / 10 = 20% of post-money.

items.definition: Reduction of a shareholder's stake due to the issuance of new shares.
items.example: Founders go from 100% to 80% after a 20% round.

items.definition: Maximum valuation used to convert a SAFE or convertible note into shares.
items.example: A 5 M€ cap protects the investor if the next round is priced at 15 M€.

items.definition: Table listing shareholders, their shares and their percentages on a given basis.
items.example: The cap table shows 60% founders, 10% pool and 30% investors.

items.definition: Computational base including all potential shares: issued, granted options and reserved pool.
items.example: Fully diluted founder ownership is lower than ownership on issued shares.

items.definition: Shares reserved for future employees and executives, usually before a round.
items.example: A pool of 10% of post-money is created before the Series A.

items.definition: Plan granting options or shares to employees, with vesting rules.
items.example: The ESOP grants 1% of capital to the first engineers.

items.definition: Gradual acquisition of rights over shares or options, often over four years with a cliff.
items.example: Options vest over 4 years with a 1-year cliff.

items.definition: Document setting out the main terms of an investment before the final legal documentation.
items.example: The term sheet provides for 6 M€, a 24 M€ pre-money and a 1x preference.

items.definition: Right to receive a priority amount on an exit before ordinary shareholders.
items.example: A 1x preference of 4 M€ is repaid before the founders.

items.definition: Preferred share that receives its preference then participates in the residual pro rata.
items.example: The investor receives 2 M€ then 20% of the residual.

items.definition: Preferred share that receives its preference or converts into ordinary shares, but does not do both.
items.example: The investor compares 2 M€ of preference with 1.2 M€ of conversion.

items.definition: Situation where liquidation preferences absorb a large share of the exit proceeds, leaving little or nothing for ordinary shares.
items.example: A 5 M€ exit leaves nothing for the founders after 6 M€ of preferences.

items.definition: Anti-dilution that adjusts an investor's conversion price to the new round's price, with no weighted average.
items.example: A down round at 50% of the previous price doubles the investor's share count.

items.definition: Anti-dilution formula that accounts for the number of new and old shares to adjust the conversion price.
items.example: Broad-based weighted average dilutes less than full ratchet.

items.definition: Round raised at a valuation lower than the previous round's.
items.example: A down round often triggers anti-dilution and pay-to-play.

items.definition: Clause forcing existing investors to participate in the new round or lose certain rights.
items.example: Investors that do not participate see their shares converted into ordinary shares.

items.definition: Discount rate that zeroes the NPV of the cash flows; measures annualised return.
items.example: A 3x MOIC over 4 years corresponds to an IRR of about 31.6%.

items.definition: Total value received divided by invested capital, without annualisation.
items.example: 10 M€ received for 2 M€ invested gives a 5x MOIC.

items.definition: Total value to paid-in capital: (distributions + residual value) / contributions.
items.example: A 1.4x TVPI means 1.4 € of total value per euro called.

items.definition: Distributions to paid-in capital: cash already distributed / contributions.
items.example: A 0.6x DPI means 60% of called capital has been returned in cash.

items.definition: Residual value to paid-in capital: residual value / contributions.
items.example: A 0.8x RVPI means 80% of capital is still invested.
